segments.voice: Yesterday a starving sage stole forbidden food in a real emergency, and the man he stole from defended dharma. Your line was a dead sage helps no one.
screen: `SHANTI AND ANUSHASANA.` · `WHEN THE RULES RUN OUT.`

segments.voice: A storm breaks over the forest. A hunter, a hard man who lives by trapping birds, is caught out in it, soaked and shaking with cold. In his cage is a female pigeon he caught that day. He crouches under a big tree for shelter, not knowing the tree is her home. Up in its branches her mate is grieving, wondering where she's gone. And from inside the cage, she can hear him. Yudhishthira had asked about a person who gives shelter to someone who asks for it. This is the story Bhishma tells.
screen: `A STORM IN THE FOREST.` → `A HUNTER UNDER THEIR TREE.` → `SHE HEARS HER MATE.`

segments.voice: The female pigeon calls up to her mate, and what she says is startling. Don't grieve for me. This man has come to our home, cold and hungry. He's our guest. Treat him as one. And the male pigeon does. He fetches a burning ember from somewhere, gathers dry leaves, and makes a fire so the hunter can warm himself. Then he realizes he has nothing to feed his guest, no store of grain, nothing set aside. So he offers himself, and drops into the fire, so the hunter will have food. The hunter is undone. The man who caught birds for a living has just watched a bird give its life to feed him. He opens the cage and lets the female go. But she, grieving her mate, follows him into the fire too, and the story says the two rise to heaven together, shining. The hunter can't go back to who he was. He throws away his nets and his cage, gives up hunting, and goes into the forest to live in austerity. The word underneath all this is atithi, the guest. In the dharma Bhishma teaches, a guest at your door is to be honored, whoever they are, even an enemy, even the person who hurt you. It's an extreme story, and the text tells it as extreme. Bhishma isn't asking the new king to leap into fires. He's showing how far hospitality reaches: past fairness, past safety, all the way to the person who did you harm.
screen: `"HE IS OUR GUEST"` · `A FIRE FOR THE HUNTER` · `THE PIGEON GIVES HIMSELF` · then, large: `THE HUNTER LAYS DOWN HIS NETS`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open and bring to mind someone who will come through your door, or your inbox, or your day, who isn't easy to welcome. As they arrive in your mind, offer them something small, warmth, a seat, a glass of water, your full attention; nothing heroic, just one real welcome. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer.
atithi. Guest: the one who comes to your door, to be honored, whoever they are, even the person who hurt you.

what a scholar hears: the story sits in Bhishma's teaching on dharma in distress, and it turns a hunter's cruelty into renunciation through a guest-offering.

chat.says: Why would a pigeon feed the very hunter who trapped his mate?

Because the pigeon hoped the hunter would pay him back by setting her free.
Because the hunter forced him, threatening to harm the female in the cage.
chat.meaning: In Bhishma's story the pigeons treat the cold, hungry hunter as atithi, a guest, and honor him even though he harmed them.
